item.research_question: How can atomic-level complexity in complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) be quantitatively engineered to predict and maximize solid-solution strengthening without relying on computationally expensive electronic structure calculations for every new composition?
item.material_system: 3d transition metal CCAs (V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) and a specific binary NiV solid solution (63.2 at.% Ni, 36.8 at.% V)
item.processing_route: Arc melting of 99.9% purity ingredients under Ti-gettered Argon; suction casting into water-cooled copper molds; homogenization at 1050–1200 °C for 24 h; cold rolling (70–85% reduction); recrystallization annealing in Ar followed by water quenching; for NiV specifically: cold rolling to 30% reduction, homogenization at 1075 °C for 45 h, cold rolling to 60% reduction, and annealing at 920 °C for 3 min.
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature with an engineering strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1; grain size of the NiV sample was 8.1 µm; comparison alloys (CrCoNi, CrMnFeCoNi) had similar grain sizes.
key_findings: The yield strength of the binary NiV solid solution is approximately 750 MPa, which is nearly double that of the Cantor high-entropy alloy (CrMnFeCoNi).

Solid-solution strengthening (σSS) in 3d CCAs is proportional to the configurational fluctuation of atomic-level pressure (ΔPsolute), with a correlation coefficient indicating a clear proportional relationship.

The atomic-level pressure in 3d CCAs is driven primarily by charge transfer (dQ) rather than atomic size difference, as the order of pressure (Cr<Mn<Fe<Co<Ni) is opposite to the order of pure atomic sizes.

The macroscopic difference in charge transfer among elements (Δelement(dQ)) is approximately 2.0 to 2.4 times larger than the average configurational difference within elements, allowing prediction of local fluctuations from elemental averages.
Solid-solution strengthening can be rationalized and predicted using the electronegativity difference (Δχ) among constituent elements, where NiV has a Δχ of 0.169 compared to 0.080 for CrMnFeCoNi.

Mixing entropy (ΔSmix) is not strongly correlated with solid-solution strengthening; alloys with lower mixing entropy (like binary NiV) can exhibit higher strength if they have a large electronegativity difference.
The ultimate tensile strength of the developed NiV alloy is close to 1200 MPa.
item.mechanism: Solid-solution strengthening originates from the configurational fluctuation of atomic-level pressure, which arises from charge transfer between neighboring elements. This charge transfer creates local electronic energy variations that interact with the elastic field of dislocations. The magnitude of this fluctuation can be approximated by the electronegativity difference among the constituent elements, which serves as a proxy for the average charge transfer and its variance.
item.limitations: The prediction of solid-solution strength does not account for other micromechanical strengthening mechanisms such as grain boundary strengthening, which contributed 2/3 of the yield strength in CrMnFeCoNi. The study assumes random chemical mixtures, though short-range order may exist and could be favored in alloys with high Δχ.
item.future_work: Further studies are required to explore quantitative relationships between atomic-level pressure, charge transfer, and various deformation mechanisms including grain boundary strengthening and thermal activation barriers. The authors suggest that charge transfer may also dominate lattice strain energy and phase stability, warranting further investigation into these electronic-to-macro couplings.
quotes: This approach can be used for designing alloys with customized properties, such as a simple binary NiV solid solution whose yield strength exceeds that of the Cantor high-entropy alloy by nearly a factor of two.

The dominant factor for solid-solution strengthening in single phase face-centered cubic (fcc) CCAs consisting of 3d transition metal elements (V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni) (3d CCAs) is the variation in the atomic-level pressures originating from the charge transfer between neighboring elements.
The yield strength of the NiV solid solution alloy is about 750 MPa and the ultimate tensile strength is close to 1200 MPa, notably outperforming the previous CCAs.
